text: A regression model gives you a number for every row, so the natural question is: how wrong are those numbers? There's no single answer. Different metrics measure different kinds of wrong, and the right one depends on what a mistake actually costs your business. This lesson covers the four you'll use most.

Mean absolute error is the average of the absolute errors, in the target's own units — MAE 10,000 means predictions are off by about $10,000 on average, every dollar counting equally. Root mean squared error squares the errors, averages them, and takes the square root — also in the target's units, but squaring makes big misses count far more than small ones.

R-squared is the share of the target's variation the model explains relative to always predicting the mean — 1.0 is perfect, 0 is no better than the mean, and it can go negative on test data when a model is worse than the mean. MAPE is the average absolute error as a fraction of the actual value — easy to explain as off by 3.5 percent on average, but it blows up near zero.
Five illustrative house prices, each prediction off by exactly $10,000: MAE and RMSE agree at 10,000, since every error is identical in size, and MAPE comes out to 3.5 percent.

Now change just the last prediction so it's off by $150,000 instead of $10,000. MAE rises from 10,000 to 38,000. RMSE jumps all the way to 67,676, because the squared error of that one large miss dominates completely. R-squared collapses from 0.98 to just 0.084.

The exact same single error is seen very differently by each metric. If large misses are especially costly, favor RMSE. If all errors cost about the same per dollar, MAE is the more direct and robust choice. Report MAE or RMSE for a dollar-scale story stakeholders understand, use R-squared alongside an error metric, and use MAPE only when the target stays well above zero.

Always compute metrics on held-out data, and compare against a simple baseline like predicting the mean. But a single number can hide a systematic problem — plot the residuals against the predictions. If the model is adequate, residuals scatter randomly around zero.

Here the true relationship is curved, but we fit a straight line. The training R-squared looks healthy at 0.968, and yet the residuals form a clear U shape — the line under-predicts at both ends and over-predicts in the middle. That pattern is a signal to add a squared feature or use a more flexible model.

The score looked good; the plot told the truth. To recap: MAE is the average miss, RMSE punishes large misses, R-squared is the share of variation explained, and MAPE is the average percentage miss. Choose based on the cost of errors, evaluate on held-out data, and always look at the residuals. Next, we turn from predicting numbers to predicting categories with logistic regression.
